Where it began

Navjot Singh Sidhu was born in Patiala, in Punjab, on 20 October 1963. He went to Yadavindra Public School in his home town and later studied commerce in Mumbai. His first-class career began in November 1981, opening for Punjab against Services at Amritsar, and he marked the day with 51.

A hundred for North Zone against the touring West Indians in 1983 earned him a Test call that November. That first taste was short, and a newspaper columnist wrote him off as a batter without a single shot. It stung, and he later said it was the making of him.

The player

He came back four years later at the 1987 World Cup and made four fifties in a row in his first four one-day internationals, a feat nobody had managed before. The same columnist who had mocked him went on to write in praise of his hitting. His return to Test cricket came in Bangalore in November 1988, with a hundred against New Zealand that helped India to a big win.

Across 51 Tests from 1983 to 1999 he made 3,202 runs at 42.13, with nine hundreds and 15 fifties. His one double hundred, 201 against the West Indies at Port of Spain in 1997, took 488 balls and was one of the most patient in Test history. In 136 one-day games he was the first Indian to pass five hundreds, and the innings he rated above all the others was an unbeaten 134 against England in Gwalior, in 1993.

What made him special

Spinners did not enjoy him. He loved to hit them over the top, once hitting eight sixes in an innings of 124 against Sri Lanka. Against the Australians in 1997–98 he made four fifties in five innings and seemed to save his best for Shane Warne.

His fielding took longer to arrive. Early on it was nothing special, but he worked at it so hard that by the end of his career team-mates had named him after Jonty Rhodes, the finest fielder of the day.

Away from the middle

His friends in the dressing room called him Sherry, and the crowds called him Sixer Sidhu. After he retired in 1999 he turned to commentary, starting on India's tour of Sri Lanka in 2001, and his colourful one-liners became so well loved that they were known as Sidhuisms. A broadcaster even ran a website where fans voted for the best of them.

Television followed, as a judge on comedy shows and for years as a guest on the programmes of Kapil Sharma, and he returned to IPL commentary in 2024. He also went into public life, winning election for Amritsar in 2004.

And finally

A comedian built a whole show on MTV around a Sidhu lookalike, complete with his own brand of one-liners. Few cricketers have had their way with words copied quite so faithfully.
